Dor
DOR
proper noun
Hebrew Dor, perhaps “dwelling” or “generation,” a royal Canaanite city on the Mediterranean coast.

Biblical Definition

Dor was a royal Canaanite city on the seacoast south of Mount Carmel, called also Naphoth-dor, “the heights of Dor.” Its king was among those that gathered to Jabin king of Hazor in the great northern confederacy against Israel, and he perished with the rest when the LORD delivered them into Israel’s hand (Josh 11:2; 12:23). The city fell within the inheritance of Manasseh, though it lay in the territory of Asher and Issachar (Josh 17:11). Yet Manasseh could not drive out the inhabitants, “but the Canaanites would dwell in that land” (Judg 1:27); the strong coastal city was only made tributary, never fully cleansed. In Solomon’s reign Dor and its region formed one of the twelve districts that provided victuals for the king’s household, governed by the son of Abinadab who had Solomon’s daughter to wife (1Ki 4:11). Dor is remembered chiefly as one of the places where Israel failed to complete the conquest, leaving the Canaanite in the land to become a snare. It witnesses that a half-finished obedience leaves a thorn that will prick the people for generations.

Webster 1828 Definition

A royal Canaanite seacoast city south of Carmel; in Manasseh’s lot, but its Canaanites were never driven out.

DOR, a royal Canaanite city on the Mediterranean coast south of Mount Carmel.

Its king joined Jabin’s northern league against Israel and was destroyed (Josh 11:2; 12:23).

It fell to Manasseh, though it lay among the coasts of Asher and Issachar (Josh 17:11).

Manasseh could not drive out its Canaanites, who dwelt there still (Judg 1:27).

It headed one of Solomon’s twelve provision districts (1Ki 4:11).

Key Scripture

Josh 12:23 — "The king of Dor in the coast of Dor, one; the king of the nations of Gilgal, one;"

Josh 17:11 — "And Manasseh had in Issachar and in Asher Bethshean and her towns, and Ibleam and her towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and her towns, and the inhabitants of Endor and her towns, and the inhabitants of Taanach and her towns, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and her towns, even three countries."

Judg 1:27 — "Neither did Manasseh drive out the inhabitants of Bethshean and her towns, nor Taanach and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Dor and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Ibleam and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Megiddo and her towns: but the Canaanites would dwell in that land."

1Ki 4:11 — "The son of Abinadab, in all the region of Dor; which had Taphath the daughter of Solomon to wife:"

Modern Corruption

A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that an unfinished obedience leaves a Canaanite in the land.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the danger of partial conquest. Manasseh defeated the king of Dor but failed to dispossess the people, choosing tribute over obedience. So the believer who spares a besetting sin, making peace with what God commanded him to put to death, leaves a thorn that will wound him and his children after him.

Dor stands among the long list of Judges 1 where the tribes “could not” drive out the Canaanites — a could-not that the narrative shows to be a would-not, a failure of faith and resolve rather than mere weakness. The LORD had promised the land; the fault lay in Israel’s slackness, not in any lack on God’s part.

Hebrew Roots

The name may mean “dwelling” or “generation,” fixed to a coastal stronghold known for its heights.

expand to see more

Dor — Hebrew Dor, perhaps “dwelling” or “generation.”

It was also called Naphoth-dor, “the heights of Dor.”

It stood on the seacoast south of Mount Carmel.

It belonged to Manasseh though set among Asher and Issachar.

The coastal stronghold was subdued but never wholly cleansed.

Usage

"Like Manasseh at Dor, the soul that makes a sin tributary instead of destroying it keeps an enemy within its border."

"Dor teaches that a victory left half-won becomes a snare in the next generation."

"The Canaanite who would dwell in the land is the picture of every sin Israel was content to spare."
